title: The child at the well
hookLine: Mencius: anyone who sees a child about to fall into a well feels alarm, and that is the seed of goodness (Mencius 2A.6)

lines: A PICTURE YOU SEE IN AN INSTANT.
cards: Are people basically good? Or basically selfish, and just good at hiding it? The news on a bad day will give you one answer.
A stranger carrying your groceries will give you the other. A Chinese philosopher named Mencius answered with a picture you can see in an instant.
It opens a week of many houses: China, India, the Sikh Gurus, the Gospels and the Buddha, one story from each, each kept by its own people.

teach.h: MENCIUS, IN THE LINE OF CONFUCIUS.
teach.b: Mencius was a teacher in the line of Confucius, and later tradition called him the second sage, honored next to Confucius himself. The book of his teachings is simply called the Mencius.
Every person, he says, has a heart that can't bear to see others suffer.
His proof: suppose someone suddenly sees a small child about to fall into a well. Anyone would feel a jolt of alarm and distress. Then he rules out the other explanations one by one.
It isn't to get in good with the child's parents.

teach.h: NOT FOR PRAISE, NOT FOR THANKS.
teach.b: It isn't to win praise from neighbors and friends. It isn't because you'd dislike what people would say, or, as some read the line, the sound of the child crying. It's there before any of that.
Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say everyone runs and saves the child. The picture stops at the jolt, the first flash, before any decision.

That flash, Mencius says, is a sprout. He names four: the heart of compassion, the heart of shame, the heart of courtesy, and the heart that knows right from wrong. Everyone has them, like having four limbs.
But sprouts have to be grown, like a small fire catching or a spring starting to flow. Not every Confucian agreed.
A later thinker named Xunzi argued the opposite: that goodness has to be trained into people from the outside. Chinese tradition kept both voices.
In Mencius's telling, a flinch at someone else's pain isn't weakness, and it isn't for show.

how: Students of Confucian thought learn the child at the well as Mencius's case that human nature is good, and read it alongside Xunzi's opposite view.

o: a new student just starting to learn
a good deed done to win people's praise
the first flash of care, before any reason

games.q: what's inside the teaching — tap the pairs.
p: a teacher in the line of Confucius

s: Mencius says everyone would save the child
he stops at the first jolt of alarm, before any decision.
Mencius rules out wanting praise as the reason
and wanting the parents' favor, and one more motive that readers take as fear of a bad name or dislike of the child's cry.
every Confucian agreed that human nature is good
Xunzi argued the opposite, and the tradition kept both voices.

games.q: you're Mencius, asked to prove people have a heart for others. what do you offer?
o: a child about to fall into a well
games.why: a child about to fall into a well. anyone would feel alarm, he says, not for praise or favor, and that jolt is the sprout of goodness.

practice: Think back over the last day or two for a moment when something in you leaned toward someone else: a wince when a friend was hurt, a wish to help a stranger, a flash of care before you thought about it.
Don't judge whether you acted on it; just notice it was there before any reasons arrived. That's one of Mencius's sprouts, so let your attention rest on it, like sun on a seedling.

wordCard.voice: Sprout. Mencius's name for the jolt of compassion anyone feels before any reason, the first sign of goodness inside us.

orig.note: Chinese, ceyin zhi xin: the heart of compassion, the first of Mencius's four sprouts.

carryVoice: Your line: the seed is there. Like any sprout, it still needs growing. See you tomorrow.
